::: {.lead}
Today you work like in a lab: you do four experiments in Word and record
what you see. You start with a plain notice and make it clear and easy to
read. Do each experiment when your teacher shows it. After each step, write
your result in its box. At the end, copy your key results into the table.
:::

## Before you start

- **You need:** a computer with Word (the desktop app, or Word on the web
  at `office.com`) and the two start files in Downloads.
- **Time:** about 40 minutes for the four experiments.
- **Check:** the results are at the end of this worksheet. On the
  interactive lesson, every step has "Check your result". Look only after
  you try.

{{< start-files >}}

## Experiment 1 · Text and paragraph formatting

**Aim:** see which commands change only the selected text, and which change
a whole paragraph. *(Lesson notes 4.1 · about 10 minutes)*

1. Open `book-fair-start.docx` in Word. If a yellow bar says *Protected
   View*, click **Enable Editing**. In the last line, *Entry to the fair is
   free for everyone.*, select only the word **free**. Click **Bold**
   (Home › Font).

   {{< record "What is bold now?" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   Only the word **free**. Text formatting (Home › Font) changes only the
   text that you select.
   :::

2. Click in the same line, but select nothing. Click **Center** (Home ›
   Paragraph).

   {{< record "What moved to the center?" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   **The whole line.** Paragraph formatting (Home › Paragraph) changes the
   whole paragraph. A click inside it is enough.
   :::

3. Press **Ctrl + A** to select the whole notice. Open **Line and Paragraph
   Spacing** (Home › Paragraph) and choose **1.5**.

   {{< record "What happens to the lines?" lines=2 >}}

   ::: {.check}
   The lines move apart, so the text is easier to read, and the notice gets
   longer. 1.15 is a smaller change that many reports use.
   :::

## Experiment 2 · Styles and headings

**Aim:** give headings a style, and see what a style does for the whole
document. *(Lesson notes 4.2 · about 10 minutes)*

1. Click in the first line, *Book Fair at the College Library*, and choose
   the style **Title** (Home › Styles). Then give the style **Heading 1** to
   the four headings: *When and where*, *What you can bring*, *How to swap a
   book* and *Prices*.

   {{< record "How do the four headings look now?" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   Bigger and in a colour (often blue). All four look the same, because
   they have the same style.
   :::

2. Open **View › Navigation Pane**. Click *Prices* in the pane.

   {{< record "The pane shows … headings; a click on Prices …" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   **4 headings**, the four with Heading 1. The title is not in the list:
   Title is not a heading style. A click on *Prices* jumps to that heading.
   :::

3. In **Home › Styles**, right-click **Heading 1** and choose **Modify**.
   Choose a green font colour and click **OK**.

   {{< record "What happens to the headings?" lines=2 >}}

   ::: {.check}
   **All four headings turn green at once.** You changed the style one
   time, and all the text with this style changed.
   :::

## Experiment 3 · A list and a table

**Aim:** choose bullets or numbers, and put information in rows and
columns. *(Lesson notes 4.3 · about 10 minutes)*

1. Look at the three lines under *What you can bring* and the three lines
   under *How to swap a book*. One group needs **Bullets**, the other
   **Numbering** (Home › Paragraph). Decide, and do it.

   {{< record "Bullets for … ; numbers for … , because …" lines=2 >}}

   ::: {.check}
   **Bullets** for the things to bring: they have no order. **Numbering**
   for the steps of the swap: they have an order (first, second, third).
   :::

2. Click at the end of the line *Prices* and press Enter. The prices are:
   novel 3 JD, dictionary 5 JD, notebook 1 JD. Insert a table (Insert ›
   Table) with 2 columns and the rows that you need, with a header row.
   Type *Book* and *Price (JD)* in the first row, then the three books.

   {{< record "My table has … columns and … rows" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   **2 columns and 4 rows**: 1 header row (*Book*, *Price (JD)*) and 3 rows
   for the three items.
   :::

3. Click in the last cell of the table (the price of the notebook) and
   press **Tab**.

   {{< record "What did Tab do?" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   **Word added a new row** at the end of the table. Type *Magazine* and
   *2*, or press Ctrl + Z to remove the row.
   :::

## Experiment 4 · A picture

**Aim:** add a picture, change its size and its wrapping, and describe it
with alt text. *(Lesson notes 4.4 · about 10 minutes)*

1. Click at the start of the text *The college library holds …*. Choose
   **Insert › Pictures › This Device** and open `books.png` (in Downloads).

   {{< record "Where is the picture, and where is the text?" lines=2 >}}

   ::: {.check}
   The picture sits **in the line**, like a very big letter, and the text
   goes on after it. This is *In Line with Text*, the first wrapping of a
   new picture.
   :::

2. Drag a **corner** handle of the picture to make it smaller (about 5 cm
   wide). Then drag a **side** handle, look at the books, and press
   **Ctrl + Z**.

   {{< record "Corner: … ; side: …" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   A **corner** keeps the shape. A **side** handle stretches the picture,
   and the books look too wide or too thin.
   :::

3. Click **Layout Options** (the small button next to the picture) and
   choose **Square**.

   {{< record "What does the text do now?" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   The text **flows around the picture**. With Square, the picture and the
   text share the lines.
   :::

4. Right-click the picture and choose **View Alt Text** (in some versions
   **Edit Alt Text**). Write the alt text in a few words.

   {{< record "My alt text" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   A good answer: a few words that say what the picture shows, for example
   "Colourful books on a wooden shelf". A screen reader reads it aloud for
   people who cannot see the picture.
   :::
